{
    "id": "12-data/cohort-analysis",
    "title": "Cohort Analysis",
    "category": "12-data",
    "level": "basic",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Segment records into cohorts by a shared anchor event, measure retention and behavior across periods, and compare cohort trajectories with explicit handling of censoring and cohort size.",
    "body": "Cohort Analysis Category: Data | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Cohort analysis compares groups defined by when they started, not by who they are. The skill covers assigning entities to cohorts by their first anchor event, binning cohorts by the calendar rule, computing period-by-period retention relative to cohort size, and censoring the trailing periods where not enough time has elapsed to observe the window. Comparisons are always normalized rates with cohort sizes attached, never raw counts. When to Use Use when behavior must be compared across groups defined by a starting event: signup month, first purchase, activation week, or onboarding batch. Do not compare raw counts across cohorts of different sizes. Normalize to rates and report cohort sizes alongside every comparison. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Timestamped records with an entity key and an event type | | | | Yes | The anchor event and the binning rule defining cohort membership | | | | No | Number of periods after the anchor to measure; bounded by default | Procedure 1. Assign each entity to a cohort by its first occurrence of the anchor event. 2. Bin cohorts by the rule in the definition: calendar month, week, or event index. 3. For each cohort, compute the size at the anchor and the survivors in each later period. 4. Convert counts to rates relative to cohort size; never report raw counts alone. 5. Flag censored trailing periods where not enough time has elapsed to observe the window . 6. Compare trajectories across cohorts and annotate every difference with cohort sizes. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Cohorts by period with sizes and survivor counts | | | | Per-cohort retention rates over the measured periods | | | | Periods excluded from comparison for insufficient elapsed time | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Survivorship bias | Only fully observed histories compared | Include censored periods and mark them in every chart | | Small-cohort volatility | Tiny cohorts read as dramatic trends | Report sizes and aggregate tiny cohorts before comparing | | Anchor event misdefined | Cohorts assigned by first record instead of the anchor | Validate the anchor against a hand-checked sample | | Period edge effects | Partial trailing period treated as complete | Mark incomplete windows as censored, not as zero | | Timezone drift | Cohort bins shift at month boundaries | Fix a timezone before binning and keep it fixed | Security and Authority Boundary Cohort tables aggregate personal behavior. Use the minimum viable entity key, avoid rejoining identifiers after aggregation, and publish rates rather than raw per-entity histories wherever the decision allows. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The pandas pivot table reference used to build cohort tables (https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/refere nce/api/pandas.DataFrame.pivottable.html). 2. The Wikipedia article defining cohort studies (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohortstudy). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. {
    "id": "12-data/data-anonymization",
    "title": "Data Anonymization",
    "category": "12-data",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Transform data sets to reduce re-identification risk using suppression, generalization, and pseudonymization, with k-anonymity checks and honest reporting of residual risk.",
    "body": "Data Anonymization Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Anonymization is measured, not declared. The skill covers classifying fields into direct identifiers, quasi-identifiers, and sensitive attributes, applying the policy of transforms, then measuring what remains: equivalence-class sizes over quasi-identifier combinations, records below threshold, and utility lost to generalization. Output that cannot meet the threshold is suppressed or further generalized rather than passed through with a false label. When to Use Use when data containing personal or identifying elements must be shared, published, or analyzed outside its origin context. Do not treat column deletion as anonymization. Remaining quasi-identifiers such as postcode, timestamps, and rare value combinations re-identify most individuals when combined. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Records containing direct or quasi-identifying fields | | | | Yes | Field-level transforms and the risk threshold the output must meet | | | | No | Re-identification checks to run; defaults to k-anonymity over quasi-identifiers | Procedure 1. Classify every field as direct identifier, quasi-identifier, sensitive, or neutral before transforming. 2. Apply the policy: suppress or tokenize direct identifiers and generalize quasi-identifiers. 3. Measure residual risk, including k-anonymity over every quasi-identifier combination. 4. Report the equivalence-class distribution and the records that fall below t he threshold. 5. Suppress or further generalize below-threshold records instead of passing them through. 6. Document the transforms applied so the output can never be presented as raw source data. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Transformed records meeting the stated threshold | | | | Equivalence-class distribution and residual risk figures | | | | Per-field transforms applied, for reproducibility and auditing | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Re-identification through combination | Quasi-identifiers generalized too coarsely | Measure k over combinations, not per field | | Over-generalization | Utility destroyed to satisfy the threshold | Tune per-field granularity and report the loss | | Pseudonyms reversed | Mapping table shipped with the output | Keep the mapping separate and access-controlled | | Linkage across releases | Same generalization used in two published sets | Vary bins across releases or use privacy-preserving models | | Free-text leakage | Names remain inside narrative fields | Scan and redact unstructured text, not just columns | Security and Authority Boundary Anonymization failures cause irreversible privacy harm. Never claim the output is anonymous without measuring residual risk, keep re-identification mapp ings under separate access control, and stop and escalate when the threshold cannot be met instead of shipping weakly protected data. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The NIST guide to de-identifying government data sets (https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/188/final). 2. The NIST Privacy Framework (https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it.     "category": "12-data",

    "description": "Define and enforce machine-readable data contracts covering schema, types, ranges, and freshness, failing production pipelines loudly when producers drift from the agreed shape.",
    "body": "Data Contract Enforcement Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A data contract is an executable agreement between a producer and a consumer. The skill covers expressing the contract as code: field names, types, ranges, nullability, and freshness expectations, then enforcing it at handoff boundaries so that a producer change surfaces as a loud, attributable failure in the producer pipeline rather than silent corruption downstream. Failures are reported with the violated clause, not a generic schema error. When to Use Use when a data set crosses a team or system boundary and downstream consumers must be protected from silent schema and quality drift. Do not enforce contracts only in tests. Without enforcement at the production handoff, producers can ship breaking changes at any time and consumers absorb them silently. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Machine-readable schema, types, ranges, and freshness rules | | | | Yes | The batch or stream being validated at the boundary | | | | No | (default) or for low-trust transitions | Procedure 1. Express the contract in code: fields, types, ranges, nullability, and freshness windows. 2. Version the contract and record which version each producer declares. 3. Validate the incoming data set at the handoff boundary, collecting every violation. 4. Fail or quarantine the batch on violation; never pass degraded data through as if clean. 5. Report violations by clau se with producer, contract version, and offending records. 6. Negotiate contract changes as versioned migrations with consumer sign-off before rollout. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Pass or fail verdict with the clause-level evidence | | | | Each violated rule with sample offending records | | | | The contract version the data was validated against | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Silent schema drift | Contract not enforced at the boundary | Validate at handoff, not only in tests | | Generic failure reports | Violations collapsed into one schema error | Report per clause with sample records | | Contract and code diverge | Contract edited without producer sign-off | Version contracts and review migrations | | Freshness never checked | Only structure enforced | Include freshness windows in the contract | | Quarantine fills up | Failing batches parked without owners | Alert on quarantine depth and assign triage | Security and Authority Bou ndary Contracts describe data an organization may be legally accountable for. Keep contract definitions in version control with review, log validation outcomes for audit, and never relax a contract to let a failing producer through without a recorded decision. Register outputs symmetrically: a dataset knows what it fed, so impact analysis can walk forward as easi ly as backward. 5.     "body": "Data Profiling Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Every analysis rests on beliefs about its data: that ids are unique, that the date column is a date, that the two category columns relate the way they did last quarter. Profiling replaces those beliefs with measurements: counts, distinct values, null rates, ranges, and distribution shapes, recorded per column and compared over time. The profile is not the analysis — it is the ground the analysis stands on, and a profile that changed since last week is often the whole explanation for a number that stopped making sense. When to Use Use when a dataset is new to you, before publication or reporting on it, and periodically on datasets assumed stable. Do not profile a known-stable, schema-verified table on every read; repeated profiling of unchanged data is cost without information. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The data being profiled | | | | Yes | Counts, null rates, distinct values, ranges to measure | | | | No | A prior profile to diff against | Procedure 1. Profile structure first: column names, types, row count, and how those differ from any recorded schema. 2. Measure completeness per column — null rates and default values — and distinctness: cardinality and top values. 3. Profile ranges and distributions for numeric and temporal columns, recording min, max, and shape, not just the mean. 4.     "body": "Data Validation Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Data arrives wrong more often than it arrives late: nulls where keys live, strings where numbers were promised, duplicate rows quietly doubling a metric. This skill moves checking to the boundary: constraints are declared alongside the pipeline, every batch is validated on arrival, and a violation stops the data instead of following it downstream. The essential move is declaring expectations explicitly — an undeclared constraint cannot be checked, and an unchecked constraint eventually becomes a wrong number someone acted on. When to Use Use at every ingestion boundary — files, API feeds, database extracts — and before anything feeds reporting, training, or user-visible output. Do not validate beyond what consumers depend on; a constraint nobody relies on still costs every batch and fails runs for no operational reason. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The batch or table arriving at the boundary | | | | Yes | Declared types, required fields, and nullability | | | | Yes | Value rules — ranges, enums, uniqueness, cross-field logic | Procedure 1. Declare the schema first — column names, types, nullability — and version it beside the pipeline that enforces it. 2. Add value constraints that consumers actually rely on: ranges, enum membership, uniqueness of keys, referential joins. 3. Run validation on arrival, per batch, and collect all violations rather than stopping at the first. 4. Route failures by severity: hard violations quarantine the batch, soft ones are logged with counts and rates. 5. Report violation statistics as data — failure rates by rule over time — so drift is visible before it becomes an outage. 6. Change the schema deliberately: a constraint change ships as a reviewed edit with a migration, not as a hotfix to silence a failing rule.     "category": "12-data",

    "description": "Process new data as it arrives instead of reprocessing the whole corpus — checkpoints, watermarks, and late-arrival handling — so cost stays flat as history grows.",
    "body": "Incremental Processing Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A pipeline that recomputes everything on every run is a pipeline with a half-life: the corpus grows, the run lengthens, and the day arrives where the run no longer fits between the arrivals. This skill switches the unit of work from the dataset to the delta: the process tracks what it has already consumed, takes only the new records past that mark, and handles the stragglers — late, out-of-order, or corrected records — by explicit rule rather than by accident. When to Use Use when data arrives continuously or the corpus is large enough that full recomputation no longer fits its window — event streams, append-only logs, growing tables. Do not add incremental machinery to small, fully recomputable datasets; a full pass over a small table is simpler, idempotent by construction, and easier to reason about. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The arriving data with an ordering or event time | | | | Yes | The consumed position the run resumes from | | | | Yes | Window wait, watermark, or drop for late arrivals | Procedure 1. Pick the position marker — an offset, a timestamp, or a sequence column — that strictly advances as new data arrives. 2. Persist a checkpoint after each processed unit, and make downstream updates idempotent so a replay from the checkpoint is safe. 3. Process only records past the checkpoint, committing the new checkpoint only after the unit is durably processed. 4. Handle late arrivals by rule: bounded wait behind a watermark, correction events, or explicit drop — never by silent overwrite. 5. Measure lag — arrival time to processed time — and alarm when the checkpoint stops advancing, because a stalled marker is the failure mode. 6. Periodically reconcile the incremental result against a full recomputation, so drift between the two is caught at a known cost. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Records consumed since the previous checkpoint | | | | The new resume position, durable after commit | | | | Arrival-to-processed delay and stall detection | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Checkpoint stalls | The marker stops advancing and data piles up | Alarm on lag and on checkpoint age | | Replay damage | Reprocessing a unit double-counts downstream | Make downstream updates idempotent per event | | Late-arrival chaos | Out-of-order records dropped or duplicated silently | Apply an explicit watermark and late policy | | Full-scan relapse | The incremental path quietly recomputing everything | Track processed volume per run | | Unverified drift | Incremental result slowly diverges from truth | Reconcile periodicall y against a full recomputation | Security and Authority Boundary Incremental state is attack surface: checkpoints record positions and the process holds partial aggregates, so both must inherit the access scope of the source data, and late-arrival or correction paths — which can rewrite aggregates — deserve the same authorization checks as the primary path.     "body": "Stream Processing Category: Data | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Stream processing computes over data that never stops arriving. The skill covers partitioning by key, defining windows with explicit late-arrival policy, advancing watermarks to bound results, emitting windowed aggregates, and handling replay and failure through idempotent sinks. Correctness comes from declared semantics: at-least-once delivery with idempotent writes, or exactly-once where the engine supports transactional state. When to Use Use when events must be aggregated, joined, or alerted on as they arrive rather than in batch: telemetry, click streams, sensor feeds, or transaction flows. Do not treat an unbounded stream as if it were a growing table. Without windows and watermarks, results never finalize and memory grows without bound. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Partitioned, append-only event source with per-key ordering | | | | Yes | Window type, size, allowed lateness, and watermark policy | | | | Yes | Idempotent or transactional output destination | Procedure 1. Declare delivery semantics first: at-least-once with idempotent sinks, or exactly-once with transactional state. 2. Partition by key so per-key ordering holds; record the partitioner choice. 3. Define windows with an explicit type, size, and allowed lateness; never use defaults silently. 4. Advance watermarks from event time and emit window results when the watermark closes the window. 5. Handle late events per policy : update the result if the sink allows, or route them to a side output. 6. On failure, restore state from the checkpoint and replay from the committed offset, proving no double emission.
